# C interop

# C interop

> Calling C, and the safety rules that come with it.

## C interop

slang already transpiles to C and shells out to `cc`, so calling into
existing C libraries is a thin layer on top of that, not a new
ecosystem: declare the C function's signature, tell the linker which
library to pull in, and call it like any other function.

```slang
link "sqlite3";   // -> '-lsqlite3' on the final cc invocation

extern fn sqlite3_libversion() -> str;
println(sqlite3_libversion());
```

- **`extern fn name(params) -> ret;`** declares a C function with no
  body — it calls the real, unmangled C symbol directly. `int`,
  `i8..u64`, `f32`, `float`, `bool`, and `str` already share their C
  representation, so they marshal for free. `bytes` does not
  auto-decay (it is a boxed struct internally); pass `bytes_ptr(b)`
  and `len(b)` as two separate `rawptr`/`i32` arguments instead of
  inventing implicit multi-argument expansion for one type.
- **`rawptr`** is an opaque foreign pointer (`void *`) for handles a C
  library owns, like `sqlite3*` or `FILE*`. It can be passed around
  and compared against **`nullptr`**, nothing else — no arithmetic,
  no field access, no dereference. A `rawptr` is never GC-owned: if a
  C library allocated it, free it through another `extern fn`, not by
  letting it go out of scope.
- **`link "name";`** is a top-level directive (parsed like `import`)
  that adds `-lname` to the `cc` invocation. Non-default search paths
  go through `LIBRARY_PATH`/`CPATH`, which `cc` already honors — no
  separate slangc flag for that.
- Only types with an unambiguous C representation may cross an
  `extern fn` boundary: numeric types, `bool`, `str`, `bytes`,
  `rawptr`, and `ptr[T]` of those types. GC'd containers (`opt`,
  `result`, `map`, structs, arrays) are rejected at compile time —
  their internal layout isn't something arbitrary C code should ever
  see.

**C++ is out of scope for the compiler itself.** There's no
name-mangling/ABI support planned. Wrap the C++ library in your own
`extern "C"` shim (catching every exception at that boundary — an
uncaught C++ exception unwinding into C is undefined behavior) and
consume the shim exactly like any other C library above.

**Safety notes:**

- The collector is precise for slang values rooted at safepoints. A
  slang value whose *only* remaining reference lives in memory the GC
  cannot scan (possible with some C libraries) can be collected while
  C still holds it. Keep a live slang-side reference for the duration
  of any call that retains a pointer beyond that call.
- Callback function pointers — C calling back into slang — aren't
  supported yet.
- **Deep C libraries and the task stack.** A task's stack starts at
  8KB and grows only at slang checkpoints, which C code has none of.
  A C function that recurses or holds large locals can therefore run
  off the end of the stack buffer and corrupt the heap — a silent
  `abort()` from `malloc`, not a clean crash. The compiler-provided
  packages that wrap deep libraries grow the stack up front
  (`sl_rt_need_stack`, used by `net.tls_*` for OpenSSL and by `sql`
  for SQLite); an `extern fn` into a comparably deep library has no
  such protection, so keep C-side recursion and stack buffers small.

See `tests/ffi/` for a complete example: a small hand-written C
fixture library (`lib.c`) built as a static archive, linked and called
from a slang program exercising `extern fn`, `link`, `rawptr`,
`bytes_ptr`, and `nullptr`.

## Packages (Go/Odin style)

A **package is a directory**: every `.sl` file inside it is compiled
together into one shared namespace, as if concatenated. Import paths
resolve to a directory next to the importer, then a native package,
then `stdlib/<path>`, then a pin in `slang.project`. Only the exact
path names a native package (`"json"` is the built-in; `"lib/json"` is
a directory), and a directory shadows a native package only if it
holds `.sl` files, so a `json/` folder of fixtures does not.

```slang
import "geometry";   // binds the name "geometry" in this file's scope
import "a/b/util";   // nested paths bind as "util"
import "geometry" as geo;   // optional alias; call as geo.area(...)

println(geometry.area(3.0, 4.0));   // qualified access
println(util.format(x));
```

**Exports are explicit.** Only declarations marked with `pub` are
visible to importers; everything else is private to its package:

```slang
// geometry/shapes.sl
pub fn area(w: float, h: float) -> float { ... }   // exported
fn scale(v: float) -> float { ... }                // private

// geometry/consts.sl
pub let pi = 3.14159;   // exported package constant
let secret = 42;        // private package global
```

Rules:

- Accessing a non-`pub` member from outside is a compile error.
- Within a package, members are used unqualified: `area(1, 2)`.
- In an imported package, top-level `let` becomes a package global;
  its initializer must be a constant literal.
- The entry point is the file you pass to `slangc`; its directory is
  the main package, and its top-level statements run in order in
  `main()`. Other files of the main package share its namespace.
- Duplicate names within a package, duplicate import bindings, and
  import cycles are all compile errors.
- Symbols are mangled per package (`sl_<pkg>_<name>`), so different
  packages can safely use the same names.
- A package's name is its directory's name made an identifier: any
  character other than a letter, digit or `_` becomes `_`, and a
  leading digit gets a `p_` prefix (`app.v2` → `app_v2`, `9lib` →
  `p_9lib`). The import *binding* is still the path's last element,
  so a directory whose name is not an identifier needs an alias:
  `import "lib.v2" as lib;`.
- Different directories are always different packages, even with the
  same name: `import "a/util";` and `import "b/util" as butil;` are two
  packages, and two libraries can each have their own `util`. When
  names clash, diagnostics show the later one with a suffix
  (`util_2`); native packages and the entry package keep theirs.

See `examples/pkgdemo/` for a complete multi-package project.

External packages are pinned in `slang.project` (walked up from the
entry file). Imports stay short. `slang.lock` holds content hashes
and is written by `slangc get`, never by hand. The file needs a `name` and
a `version` line as well as its pins; `slangc new` writes both.

```
name myserver
version 0.1.0

pkg foo git https://github.com/dolphlabs/foo tag v0.1.0
pkg bar git https://github.com/dolphlabs/bar tag v0.2.0 dir src
```

```slang
import "foo";
import "bar";
```

`dir <subdir>` points a pin at the package **inside** the repository,
for a library that also ships examples, docs and its own tests: only
that directory is compiled into your program, and nothing else in the
repository can affect your build. The subdirectory is a relative path
within the clone — `..`, absolute paths and empty segments are refused —
and the lock hashes the package's complete included tree, not just the
selected source directory.

A package author can keep non-runtime directories out of every consumer's
cache by listing them in that package repository's own `slang.project`:

```
name foo
version 1.2.0
exclude bench
exclude examples
exclude tests
```

Each `exclude` is one literal repository-relative directory; paths with
`..`, absolute paths, empty segments, or glob syntax are rejected. Do not
exclude the package directory selected by a consumer's `dir`; `slangc get`
refuses that pin. A directory inside it may be excluded (test fixtures, say)
as long as the package never imports it: an import that lands in an excluded
directory is a compile error naming the `exclude` line, because otherwise
`import "json"` from a package whose own `json/` was excluded would quietly
compile the standard `json` instead. The author sees that error first: the
same check runs in the package's own repository, where the directory is
still present and the import would otherwise compile, so a broken exclude
fails the author's build rather than a consumer's. Code that never ships
is exempt there: `*_test.sl` files, and anything inside an excluded
directory (a benchmark importing the package, a test program). `slangc get`
uses a shallow partial clone and sparse checkout so a Git server that supports
partial clones need not send excluded file contents. If it does not, slang
still omits those directories and Git metadata from the local cache, but the
first transfer may include them. The lock hash covers every retained file, so
editing included source is detected before compilation. Projects without
`exclude` keep the existing full-tree behavior.

`slangc get` clones each `pkg` line into `$SLANG_CACHE/pkg/<name>/<hash>`
(`~/.cache/slang` if unset), links `$SLANG_CACHE/pkg/<name>/<tag>` to it
(a `/` in the tag becomes `_`), and prints one line per package with
that typeable path — `zokor v0.1.0: /home/you/.cache/slang/pkg/zokor/v0.1.0/src`
— for reading a package's source or docs. Builds never go through the
link; they use the lock's hash. If a fetched package has its own
`slang.project`, those pins are fetched too and recorded only in
`slang.lock`. Compile does not hit the network. A missing lock, missing
cache, or hash mismatch is an error. Same short name at two git/tag
pairs is an error.

---

slang is built and maintained by **Dolphlabs** (Dolph Tech Limited) — https://dolphlabs.com



# How it works

# How it works

> The compiler pipeline, the collector, the scheduler.

## How it works

```
main.sl ──loader──> packages ──lexer/parser──> ASTs ──codegen──> main.gen.c ──cc──> ./main
```

1. **Loader** (`src/loader.c`) — resolves imports (local directory,
   native package, stdlib, then `slang.project` pins), scans package directories for `.sl`
   files (in deterministic sorted order), merges them per package, and
   detects cycles via canonical paths.
2. **Lexer** (`src/lexer.c`) — tokenizes source into identifiers,
   keywords, literals, and operators.
3. **Parser** (`src/parser.c`) — recursive-descent parser producing an
   AST (`src/ast.h`).
4. **Code generator** (`src/codegen/`) — walks the ASTs, performs type
   inference and semantic checks (including `pub` enforcement), and
   emits readable C. The runtime in `runtime/` (GC, scheduler, pool,
   containers, native packages) is real C, spliced into every
   generated file so the binary stays self-contained. Split by
   concern: `core.c`, `infer.c`, `expr.c`/`stmt.c`, `program.c`,
   `liveness.c` (GC safepoint roots), and `native.c` (`NatSig`
   dispatch). `internal.h` holds the shared `CG` struct.

   Native-package *signatures* live under `src/codegen/pkg_<name>/`.
   Their C runtimes are `runtime/sl_<name>.c`. `json` uses
   `dispatch.c` because decode/encode are generic over the target
   type. Adding a fixed-signature package is a `pkg_<name>/` directory,
   a `runtime/sl_<name>.c` file, and one line in `loader.c`.
5. **Driver** (`src/main.c`) — glues it together and shells out to
   `cc`. Because GCC/Clang compile the generated C, you get their full
   optimizer for free.

   **Large stack frames.** A task starts on an 8KB stack that grows only at a
   safepoint, which runs after the current function's frame already exists.
   How big a frame is depends on the C compiler: clang gives every call site
   its own spill slot and inlines callees into their caller, so a function
   with a few hundred call sites can need more than the whole stack and used
   to die with `SIGBUS` before printing anything (gcc gave the same C a frame
   of a few hundred bytes). The driver therefore asks the compiler for the
   real frame of every function (`-Wframe-larger-than`, read from clang's and
   gcc's own reports). A slang function reported over the limit is
   regenerated behind a thin wrapper that grows the stack *before* the
   function is entered, and the program is compiled a second time. So is
   the C slangc generates for `json.decode`/`json.encode`, `pg.rows_as` and
   `inspect`, whose frames grow with the type: a decoder for a 200-field
   struct needs more stack than a safepoint leaves free, and without a
   guard the task ran into its guard page. The
   guards a build ends with are kept in the cache
   (`~/.cache/slang/frames/`, or `$SLANG_CACHE/frames/`, one small file per
   program) and applied up front the next time the same program is built,
   so a rebuild compiles once; every compile still checks the frames, and
   one that has outgrown its guard is regenerated as before. A guard is
   sized in whole 4KB pages, as the stack grows, so a frame that changes by
   a few bytes costs no compile. Programs with no large frame pay nothing,
   and `--emit-c` output has no guards. The limit is 1536 bytes;
   `SLANG_FRAME_LIMIT` overrides it (the tests set a tiny one to put a
   guard on nearly every function).

**Development builds.** `--dev` (or `SLANG_DEV=1` in the environment)
compiles the generated C at `-O0` without LTO, which is most of a build's
time: a 21k-line service rebuilds in about 16 s instead of 73 s. The program
runs slower (about 1.6x the CPU per request on that service), so it is for
the edit-and-rerun loop -- `zokor watch` builds this way -- and never for
what you deploy. Unoptimized frames are several times bigger, so a dev build
also starts tasks on a 32KB stack with a 16KB safepoint margin, guards
frames over 8KB, and is cached apart from the release build of the same
program.

Inspect what slang generates:

```sh
./slangc examples/hello/main.sl --emit-c && cat main.gen.c
```

## Memory management

Compiled programs embed a precise mark-sweep collector
(`runtime/sl_gc.c`). Allocations go through `sl_gc_alloc`. `main()`
registers the thread, starts the worker pool, and switches into the
main task. There is no `libgc` dependency.

What this means in practice:

- No manual memory management in slang; no leaks from string churn.
- Collection is tracing (mark-and-sweep), so reference cycles are
  collected — unlike refcounting.
- Cost: stop-the-world pauses. The allocator still serializes on a
  mutex (batched); that is the current throughput ceiling.
- Every pool worker is registered with the collector. A collection
  stops the world, walks safepoint roots, the run queue, parked
  tasks, and (for async-preempted tasks) a conservative stack scan.
- Pacing follows the live heap, like Go's default (`GOGC=100`): the next
  collection comes after allocating as much as survived the last one,
  and never before 8MB. The heap peaks near twice what is live, however
  much garbage a program makes — streaming three million database rows
  runs in under 20MB.
- Generational and non-moving: new objects start in a nursery, and a
  minor collection runs after every 512KB of allocation. The nursery
  grows, up to 2MB per worker (16MB at most), while minors take a large
  share of the time and keep finding much of it live -- a busy server
  re-marking its in-flight requests -- and shrinks back when they do not,
  so a program whose garbage dies young keeps the small footprint. It marks from
  the roots and the remembered set (old objects a write barrier saw gain
  a pointer to a young one), sweeps only the nursery, and promotes what
  survives two minors: data that is merely in use when a minor lands,
  like a request half way through, stays young and dies young instead of
  being left for a major. Old objects are never traced by a minor, so its
  cost follows the nursery, not the heap: about 0.8ms per minor whether a
  program keeps 20k or a million long-lived objects. Majors sweep
  everything and promote what they keep.
- Both kinds sweep in parallel: the threads stopped for a collection take
  a share of the heap's pages each, instead of waiting while one thread
  sweeps them all. `SLANG_GC_STAT` counts the joins (`sweep_helps`).
- A list or map whose elements hold no pointer -- numbers, `bool`, enums,
  and value structs made only of those -- is never traced at all: a
  table of a million ints costs a collection nothing to keep.
- A list or map written since the last minor is traced from the first
  position written, not from the start, so filling a million-entry list
  or map costs each minor only what was added since the previous one.
  Updating an existing map key is the exception: its position is not
  recorded, so the next minor traces that whole map.
- `SLANG_GC_STAT=1` prints collection counts and pause times at exit
  (`minor_pause_ns_total` for the minors).
  `SLANG_GC_THRESHOLD_KB=n` collects every n KB instead, with no pacing:
  for tests, since a rooting bug only shows when a collection lands at
  the one safepoint where an object is unrooted. `SLANG_GC_NURSERY_KB=n`
  does the same for minors.
- `SLANG_GC_VERIFY_MINOR=1` checks every minor against a full mark and
  reports any live young object it missed, with the kind of old
  container holding it -- a store with no write barrier. It prints
  `missed=` at exit; the suite requires 0.

## Project layout

```
src/
  common.h       allocation helpers, growable string buffer, file I/O
  loader.h/.c    package discovery, merging, cycle detection
  lexer.h/.c     tokenizer
  ast.h          AST node definitions
  parser.h/.c    recursive-descent parser
  rtpath.h/.c    locate runtime/ next to slangc
  codegen.h      public codegen API (codegen_program, and the frame guards)
  codegen/       type checking + C emission
  main.c         driver: flags, invokes cc
runtime/       real C runtime spliced into generated programs
  sl_core.c sl_gc.c sl_containers.c sl_sched.c sl_pool.c
  sl_time.c sl_net.c sl_tls.c sl_json.c sl_proc.c sl_fs.c
stdlib/        slang-source packages (`import "http"`, `import "byteutil"`;
             `import "log"` is a native package — no source files)
examples/      one directory per example program
tests/         language tests plus tests/runtime/ (no slangc)
Makefile       build/test/clean
```

slang is built and maintained by **Dolphlabs** (Dolph Tech Limited) — https://dolphlabs.com



# Limitations

# Limitations

> What slang does not do, stated plainly.

## Known limitations

- A plain `struct` cannot hold itself through an `opt` (or a `result`):
  both are held by value, so the type would be infinitely large, and the
  compiler says so. Make it a `gc struct`, which is a pointer -- that is
  how a linked list is written (`gc struct Node { v: int, next:
  opt[Node] }`).

- Block scoping: a `let` inside `if`/`else`/`while`/`for` is not
  visible afterwards. Loop bindings (`for i in ...`) are scoped to
  the loop. Redeclaring a name in the same scope is an error;
  inner blocks may shadow. `guard let` still binds for the rest of
  its enclosing block.
- Strings are immutable; concatenation allocates. The collector
  reclaims unreachable strings automatically.
- Package globals require constant-literal initializers, and cannot be
  reassigned. A package-level `bytes` is one value shared by every use:
  `G[0] = 65` (or a function handed `G` that writes to it) changes it
  for everyone, as for any `bytes` held in two places.
- Implicit returns only apply to the last statement of a function
  body; `if` and `{}` blocks are statements, not expressions yet.
- No closures. Functions are values (`fn(int) -> int`), but they
  capture nothing — a function value always names a top-level
  function, never an environment. `break`/`continue` work inside
  loops.
- Package-level lists are not supported yet (scalars and bytes are).
- Map keys are limited to integers, `str`, and `bool`.
- No data-race protection: `spawn` gives you real concurrency and
  per-task failure isolation, not an ownership/borrow checker.
  Mutating a shared struct/list/map from more than one task is on
  you, same as Go or Java — `mutex` is available for it, but nothing
  makes you reach for one.
- `select` has no timeout arm and no way to disable an arm. A closed
  channel's recv arm is ready forever (see Concurrency above), and
  there is no nil channel to switch it off with; for a deadline, feed
  a channel from a spawned timer task.
- `mutex` has no scope guard: without closures or `defer`, an early
  `return` between `mutex_lock` and `mutex_unlock` leaks the lock.
  Mutexes are also not recursive (locking one twice from the same
  task is a checked error, not a hang).
- TLS: no session resumption tuning. Handshake and send/recv park;
  `getaddrinfo` in `tls_dial` parks the task while a dedicated
  thread resolves. mTLS (`tls_ctx_require_client` /
  `tls_ctx_use_cert`) and SNI extra certs (`tls_ctx_add_sni`) are
  supported.
- JSON: no dynamic/unknown-shape decoding (every decode target is a
  concrete slang type known at compile time — see the `json` section
  above), and JSON object keys map to struct field names verbatim
  (no camelCase/snake_case conversion). `bytes` fields are base64
  strings (RFC 4648).
- `proc`: only `SIGTERM`/`SIGINT` are handled (there's no general
  signal-registration API), and only in a program that calls
  `proc.shutdown_requested()`; a second signal always ends it. A
  signal that arrives in the narrow window before `main()` takes them
  over gets the OS's default disposition (immediate termination).
  `proc.wait_idle()` parks until `proc.active_tasks()` is zero.

---

slang is built and maintained by **Dolphlabs** (Dolph Tech Limited) — https://dolphlabs.com



# builder

# builder

> Package builder.

Assembling a result one piece at a time with `+` is **quadratic**: `a + b`
allocates and copies both sides, so the cost is the sum of every
intermediate length. Building 80 KB one byte at a time takes about two
seconds, and a megabyte would take minutes. `builder` collects the pieces
and copies each once, at the end.

```slang
import "builder";

let b = builder.new_str();
b.write("hello").write(", ").write(name).write_int(42).write_line("!");
let s = b.finish();                    // one allocation, linear in the total

let y = builder.new_bytes();
y.write_byte(104).write(b"ello").write_str(" world");
let raw: bytes = y.finish();
```

`Str` is for text and `Bytes` for binary data. Both chain, report
`size()` in bytes without assembling anything, and offer `finish()` (which
can be called again after more writes), `take()` (finish and start over)
and `reset()`. The chunk is made on the first short write, so a builder
that only takes long pieces never pays for it, and `take()` hands back a
lone piece without copying it. `Bytes.write_byte` fills a 512-byte chunk in place, so a
million single-byte writes make about two thousand allocations rather than a
million: 4 million of them take 136 ms. `Bytes` keeps a **copy** of what you
write, because bytes are mutable and a later change of yours must not
rewrite what was already written.

For assembling a `[bytes]` you already hold, `strings.join_bytes(parts,
sep)` is the counterpart of `strings.join`. `bench/builder/` prints the
naive loop beside the builder.

## API

### `gc struct Str`

### `fn new_str() -> Str`

### `fn write(self: Str, s: str) -> Str`

Appends, and returns the builder so writes chain. A str is immutable, so the builder holds the caller's value, not a copy.

### `fn write_int(self: Str, n: int) -> Str`

### `fn write_line(self: Str, s: str) -> Str`

### `fn size(self: Str) -> int`

The bytes written so far, without assembling anything.

### `fn is_empty(self: Str) -> bool`

### `fn finish(self: Str) -> str`

The whole result, in one allocation. Can be called again after more writes; each call assembles what is there, so ask once when you are done rather than after every write.

### `fn take(self: Str) -> str`

finish() and start over.

### `fn reset(self: Str) -> int`

### `gc struct Bytes`

### `fn new_bytes() -> Bytes`

The chunk starts as the shared empty b"" and is made on the first short write (has_chunk): a builder that only takes long pieces, or none, never pays for it. It used to be built eagerly as a 512-byte str and then copied to bytes -- 1 KB and two allocations before any write.

### `fn write_byte(self: Bytes, b: int) -> Bytes`

### `fn write(self: Bytes, b: bytes) -> Bytes`

Appends a copy. Bytes are mutable in slang, so keeping the caller's own value would let a later change of theirs rewrite what was already written.

### `fn write_str(self: Bytes, s: str) -> Bytes`

Text goes in as its UTF-8 bytes. `to_bytes` already makes a fresh value, so a long string is kept as-is rather than copied twice.

### `fn size(self: Bytes) -> int`

### `fn is_empty(self: Bytes) -> bool`

### `fn finish(self: Bytes) -> bytes`

The whole result, in one allocation. Leaves the builder as it was, so it can be written to and finished again; call it once when you are done rather than after every write.

### `fn take(self: Bytes) -> bytes`

finish, then reset. With a single piece that piece is the result: the reset drops the builder's hold on it, so no copy is needed.

### `fn reset(self: Bytes) -> int`

---

slang is built and maintained by **Dolphlabs** (Dolph Tech Limited) — https://dolphlabs.com



# byteutil

# byteutil

> Package byteutil.

Search, trim, and split on the `bytes` type — no new syntax. The
package cannot be named `bytes` because that token is the type.

```slang
import "byteutil";

byteutil.find(b"hello", 0, 108);     // 2, or -1
byteutil.has_prefix(b"hello", b"he");
byteutil.has_suffix(b"hello", b"lo");
byteutil.trim(b"  hi\r\n");          // b"hi" (space/tab/CR/LF)
byteutil.split(b"a,b", 44);          // [b"a", b"b"]
```

## API

### `fn find(b: bytes, from: int, target: int) -> int`

Index of the first `target` byte in `b` at or after `from`, or -1 if it does not occur. `target` is a byte value, not a substring: 44 is a comma.

### `fn find_wire(b: wire, from: int, target: int) -> int`

Same directly on an arena buffer: the http head scan walks the socket wire and needs the colon position without copying the line into GC bytes first.

### `fn has_prefix(b: bytes, prefix: bytes) -> bool`

Does `b` begin with `prefix`? A prefix longer than `b` is false rather than an error.

### `fn has_suffix(b: bytes, suffix: bytes) -> bool`

Does `b` end with `suffix`? A suffix longer than `b` is false rather than an error.

### `fn trim(b: bytes) -> bytes`

`b` without leading or trailing ASCII whitespace -- space, tab, CR and LF. Returns a new `bytes`; the input is unchanged.

### `fn split(b: bytes, sep: int) -> [bytes]`

Split `b` on every occurrence of the `sep` byte. Adjacent separators yield empty elements, so the result always has one more element than there were separators.

---

slang is built and maintained by **Dolphlabs** (Dolph Tech Limited) — https://dolphlabs.com



# cache

# cache

> Package cache.

An in-process cache: string keys, any value type, bounded by entry count
(and optionally by bytes), least recently used out first, with an
optional time to live, and a loader that runs once per key however many
tasks ask at the same moment.

```slang
import "cache";

let o = cache.options();
o.max_entries = 50000;
o.ttl_ms = 30000;                                          // 0: never expires
let cr: result[cache.Cache[User], str] = cache.new(o);
guard let users = cr else let e = err_of(cr) { panic(e); }

cache.put(users, "u:42", u);
cache.get(users, "u:42");                                  // opt[User]
cache.put_ttl(users, "u:7", u7, 1000);                     // its own time to live
cache.put_sized(users, "u:9", u9, 512);                    // counts towards max_bytes
cache.remove(users, "u:42");
cache.stats(users);                                        // hits, misses, evictions, ...

let r = cache.get_or_load(users, "u:42", db, load_user);   // result[User, str]
fn load_user(db: pg.Pool, key: str) -> result[User, str] { ... }
```

**Shards.** The cache is split into shards (16 by default), each with its
own lock, hash table and recency list, so tasks on different workers
rarely wait for each other. A key is hashed once with `strings.hash`; the
low bits pick its shard. Limits are per shard (`max_entries / shards`), so
the entry evicted is the least recently used of its shard, and a cache
filled to its limit holds slightly fewer than `max_entries` when its keys
spread unevenly (998,222 of 1,000,000 in the benchmark), as in most
sharded caches.

**The table** is the shard's own open-addressing table, not a `map`:
`map`'s `del` keeps insertion order and so takes time linear in the map's
size, and a cache deletes on every eviction. The table deletes by
backward shift in constant time on average, grows at half full, and
reuses the hash that chose the shard.

**Expiry** is checked when an entry is read: an expired entry is dropped
and counted. Entries nobody reads leave as the shard's least recently used.

**Loading once.** On a miss, `get_or_load` runs the loader in its own
task; callers that ask for the same key meanwhile wait for its result. A
loader's error, or its panic's message, goes to every waiter and nothing
is cached. slang has no closures, so what the loader needs comes in as
`ctx`.

**Cost.** Linux container, 4 workers on 4 CPUs, 100,000 keys drawn
skewed, a 10,000-entry cache, 90% reads, medians of 4 rounds against Go's
`hashicorp/golang-lru/v2` (one lock) and `ristretto`:

| | slang `cache` | golang-lru | ristretto |
|---|---|---|---|
| one task, ns/op | 714 | 212 | 268 |
| 8 tasks, ns/op | 320 | 232 | 126 |
| hit rate | 21.0% | 21.0% | 3.1% |
| 1M entries, RSS | 256 MB | 198 MB | -- |

slang's hit rate matches golang-lru's (both are LRU); ristretto admits
few new keys under this skew. Most of slang's single-task gap is below
the cache: a plain `map[str]int` lookup costs 290-400 ns on the same
keys, as `str` is NUL-terminated (length, hashing and `==` walk it).
`bench/cache/run.sh` reproduces this.

## API

### `gc struct Options`

### `fn options() -> Options`

### `gc struct Stats`

### `gc struct Cache[V]`

### `fn new[V](o: Options) -> result[Cache[V], str]`

A cache with options o: an error if max_entries is below 1, max_bytes or ttl_ms negative, or shards over 4096.

### `fn get[V](c: Cache[V], key: str) -> opt[V]`

The value under key, if it is there and has not expired.

### `fn put[V](c: Cache[V], key: str, value: V)`

Puts value under key with the cache's time to live, replacing what was there.

### `fn put_ttl[V](c: Cache[V], key: str, value: V, ttl_ms: int)`

put with this entry's own time to live (0: forever).

### `fn put_sized[V](c: Cache[V], key: str, value: V, size: int)`

put of a value that counts as size bytes towards max_bytes (its key's length is added).

### `fn remove[V](c: Cache[V], key: str) -> bool`

Removes key; true if it was there.

### `fn clear[V](c: Cache[V])`

Removes every entry (the statistics stay).

### `fn len_of[V](c: Cache[V]) -> int`

Entries held, expired ones not yet dropped included.

### `fn stats[V](c: Cache[V]) -> Stats`

### `fn get_or_load[V, C](c: Cache[V], key: str, ctx: C, loader: fn(C, str) -> result[V, str]) -> result[V, str]`

The value under key; on a miss, loader(ctx, key) is run once -- however many tasks ask for key meanwhile -- and its value cached with the cache's time to live. Its error, or its panic's message, is returned to every caller waiting on it, and nothing is cached.

---

slang is built and maintained by **Dolphlabs** (Dolph Tech Limited) — https://dolphlabs.com



# compress

# compress

> Package compress.

gzip, zlib and raw DEFLATE, over zlib (`-lz`, added only when a program
imports `compress`).

```slang
import "compress";

let gr = compress.gzip(body);
guard let gz = gr else let e = err_of(gr) { log.error(e); return; }

// decompression ALWAYS takes a ceiling -- see below
let ur = compress.gunzip(payload, 4194304);        // 4 MiB
guard let plain = ur else let e = err_of(ur) {
    log.warn("rejected: " + e);                     // names the limit
    return;
}
```

| Function | Signature |
|---|---|
| `compress.gzip` | `(b: bytes) -> result[bytes, str]` |
| `compress.gzip_level` | `(b: bytes, level: int) -> result[bytes, str]` |
| `compress.gunzip` | `(b: bytes, max_out: int) -> result[bytes, str]` |
| `compress.deflate` | `(b: bytes) -> result[bytes, str]` |
| `compress.inflate` | `(b: bytes, max_out: int) -> result[bytes, str]` |
| `compress.deflate_raw` | `(b: bytes) -> result[bytes, str]` |
| `compress.deflate_raw_flush` | `(b: bytes) -> result[bytes, str]` (ends in a sync flush, no final block: RFC 7692) |
| `compress.inflate_raw` | `(b: bytes, max_out: int) -> result[bytes, str]` |
| `compress.crc32` | `(b: bytes) -> int` (the zip, gzip and PNG CRC-32) |
| `compress.crc32_update` | `(crc: int, b: bytes) -> int` (continue one over pieces) |

**Decompression takes a mandatory output limit.** `max_out` is a
required argument, not an optional one with a generous default. The
expansion ratio is unbounded — 65 KB of gzip holds 64 MB of output, and
that ratio goes much further — so a program that decompresses anything
it did not itself produce is one hostile input away from the OOM killer.
The ceiling is enforced *before* the allocation that would cross it, not
by inspecting the result afterwards: rejecting a 64 MB bomb was measured
at 3.9 MB peak RSS against a 0.86 MB baseline. A default here would be a
number nobody chose, applied at every call site that never thought about
it.

**Three containers, because HTTP needs all three.** They are the same
compressed bits under different headers: `gzip` (RFC 1952) is what
servers send; `zlib` (RFC 1950) is what the `deflate` content-coding is
*supposed* to mean; raw (RFC 1951, no header) is what the servers that
get it wrong send instead — which is why `inflate_raw` exists rather
than being a purist's omission. They are not interchangeable, and each
decoder says so rather than producing garbage.

**Backed by zlib rather than written here**, unlike `regex`. That
package was written in-house because a backtracking engine has a
catastrophic input class and being immune to it by construction was the
point. DEFLATE has no equivalent argument — what it has is thirty years
of hostile input and a reference implementation on every platform slang
targets. A hand-written inflate would be a memory-safety surface with no
upside, since every bug in one is a buffer overrun driven by
attacker-controlled input.

## API

### `compress.crc32(bytes) -> int`

### `compress.crc32_update(int, bytes) -> int`

### `compress.gzip(bytes) -> result[bytes,str]`

### `compress.gzip_level(bytes, int) -> result[bytes,str]`

### `compress.deflate(bytes) -> result[bytes,str]`

### `compress.deflate_raw(bytes) -> result[bytes,str]`

### `compress.deflate_raw_flush(bytes) -> result[bytes,str]`

### `compress.gunzip(bytes, int) -> result[bytes,str]`

### `compress.inflate(bytes, int) -> result[bytes,str]`

### `compress.inflate_raw(bytes, int) -> result[bytes,str]`

---

slang is built and maintained by **Dolphlabs** (Dolph Tech Limited) — https://dolphlabs.com



# context

# context

> Package context.

Cancellation and deadlines that flow from a request through everything
it starts, so one timeout or one cancel stops all the work under it.

```slang
import "context";
import "net";

let req = context.with_timeout(context.background(), 2000000000);  // 2 s
let db = context.with_cancel(req);          // ends when req ends
context.watch_fd(db, fd);                   // a cancel closes fd
let rr = net.recv_until(fd, 4096, context.deadline(db));
context.cancel(req, "client went away");    // ends req and db
println(context.cause(db) ?? "live");       // "client went away"
context.release(db);
```

- `background()` is the root. `with_cancel(parent)`,
  `with_timeout(parent, ns)` and `with_deadline_at(parent, mono_ns)` make
  children; a child's deadline is the earlier of its own and its
  parent's, and cancelling a context cancels everything made from it.
- `deadline(c)` is an `until` for any API that waits; `remaining(c)` is
  the nanoseconds left (-1 without a deadline), for a timeout another
  protocol carries.
- `cancel(c, reason)` (the first reason wins) and `release(c)`, for a
  context whose work is done. Call one of them, as with Go's contexts:
  until then a child stays in its parent's list.
- `is_done(c)` and `cause(c)`: the cancel reason, `"deadline exceeded"`,
  or `none` while live.
- `watch_fd(c, fd)` closes `fd` on cancel, waking a task parked on it
  with `"closed"`; `unwatch_fd` before closing it yourself. `done_chan(c)`
  is closed on cancel, for a `select`.

There are no timers: a deadline passing does not close watched fds. The
operations given `deadline(c)` end at it on their own.

## API

### `gc struct Context`

### `fn background() -> Context`

The root: no deadline, never cancelled unless cancel is called on it.

### `fn with_cancel(parent: Context) -> Context`

A child of parent that can be cancelled on its own.

### `fn with_timeout(parent: Context, ns: int) -> Context`

A child of parent that ends ns nanoseconds from now (or at the parent's deadline, if that is sooner). ns <= 0 is already past.

### `fn with_deadline_at(parent: Context, mono_ns: int) -> Context`

A child of parent that ends at mono_ns, an absolute time.mono() value.

### `fn cancel(c: Context, reason: str)`

Cancels c and every context made from it, with reason as cause's text. The first cancel wins; later ones do nothing.

### `fn release(c: Context)`

Cancel with the reason "released": for a context whose work finished.

### `fn is_done(c: Context) -> bool`

Whether c was cancelled or its deadline has passed.

### `fn cause(c: Context) -> opt[str]`

Why c is done: the cancel reason, or "deadline exceeded"; none while it is live.

### `fn deadline(c: Context) -> until`

c's deadline as an `until` for any API that waits: never for a context without one, already passed for a cancelled one.

### `fn remaining(c: Context) -> int`

Nanoseconds until c's deadline (0 once passed or cancelled), or -1 for a context without one: for a timeout another protocol carries, such as a database statement timeout.

### `fn watch_fd(c: Context, fd: i32)`

Closes fd when c is cancelled, waking any task parked on it with "closed". If c is already cancelled, closes it now. Call unwatch_fd before closing fd yourself, so a later cancel cannot close a reused fd number.

### `fn unwatch_fd(c: Context, fd: i32) -> bool`

Stops watching fd. Returns false if c had already been cancelled (and fd closed by it).

### `fn done_chan(c: Context) -> chan[bool]`

A channel that is closed when c is cancelled, for a `select` that should also end on cancellation. Nothing is ever sent on it.

---

slang is built and maintained by **Dolphlabs** (Dolph Tech Limited) — https://dolphlabs.com



# crypto

# crypto

> Package crypto.

Hashes, MACs, key derivation, authenticated encryption and signatures
over OpenSSL: SHA-256/384/512 and their HMACs, HKDF, PBKDF2, Argon2id,
AES-256-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305, Ed25519, ECDSA P-256, RSA, and a
CSPRNG. Hashes and HMACs are infallible on valid inputs and return
`bytes` directly; anything that can fail returns a `result`.

```slang
import "crypto";

let h: bytes = crypto.sha256(b"abc");              // 32 bytes
let m: bytes = crypto.hmac_sha256(key, msg);       // 32 bytes
let r = crypto.rand(32);
guard let b = r else let e = err_of(r) {
    log.error("rand failed: " + e);
}
let k = crypto.pbkdf2_sha256(password, salt, 600000, 32);   // RFC 8018
let s1: bytes = crypto.sha1(b"abc");               // 20 bytes
let d: bytes = crypto.md5(b"abc");                 // 16 bytes
```

`pbkdf2_sha256(password, salt, iterations, length)` accepts 1 to
10,000,000 iterations and a length of 1 to 1024 bytes; anything else is
an `err`. The iteration count is capped because it is often chosen by the
other side of a protocol (a SCRAM server sends it) and the whole
derivation runs without yielding the worker thread.

`sha1` and `md5` are broken for collision resistance. They exist for the
protocols that still specify them and cannot be changed -- the WebSocket
handshake (RFC 6455) hashes the client's key with a fixed GUID, Git
object ids, Postgres md5 authentication, `Content-MD5`,
legacy ETags -- and must not protect anything new.

The low-level `argon2id_raw` and `argon2id_verify` primitives support the
standalone [`argon` package](https://github.com/dolphlabs/argon), which emits
standard PHC password hashes. They accept byte passwords and salts and
validated cost parameters; verification returns `ok(false)` for a mismatch
and compares tags in constant time. Calls require OpenSSL 3.2 or newer with
Argon2id support; on older OpenSSL builds they return an error while the
other `crypto` functions remain available. Use the package's bounded PHC
parser rather than parsing stored hashes in application code.

A derivation is tens of milliseconds of work that cannot be preempted. In
a program that links the reactor (anything importing `net` or `io`, so
every server), it runs on a small pool of dedicated kdf threads while the
calling task parks, the way a DNS lookup does: a burst of logins neither
pins the pool's workers nor holds up a collection. `SLANG_KDF_THREADS`
sets the pool size (default: one per worker). Each in-flight derivation
holds its `memory_kib`, so bound how many you start, as you would any
other expensive request. Without the reactor it derives on the calling
worker.

`bcrypt_verify(password, hash) -> result[bool, str]` and
`scrypt(password, salt, n, r, p, length) -> result[bytes, str]` are for
password hashes carried over from other systems (Rails, Laravel and
Django use bcrypt; Django also scrypt), until each user logs in again
and can be re-hashed with Argon2id. Neither is for new hashes.

```slang
let ok_v = crypto.bcrypt_verify(b"hunter2", "$2y$12$...") ?? false;   // $2a$ $2b$ $2y$
let key = crypto.scrypt(b"pw", b"salt", 16384, 8, 1, 64);              // RFC 7914
```

`bcrypt_verify` reads `$2a$`, `$2b$` and `$2y$` with costs 04 to 18 (a
stored hash names its own cost, so it is capped) and only the first 72
bytes of the password, as bcrypt does; `$2x$` and the original `$2$` are
an `err`. scrypt takes N a power of two up to 2^20, r up to 32, p up to
16, at most 256 MiB (128 * N * r bytes) and 1 to 64 bytes out. Both run
on the kdf threads like Argon2id. bcrypt is eksblowfish written here
(OpenSSL has none); scrypt is OpenSSL's.

`rsa_verify_sha256(n, e, msg, sig) -> result[bool, str]` checks an
RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 SHA-256 signature (JWS `RS256`) against a public key
given as its raw big-endian modulus and exponent, which is what a JWKS
entry's base64url `n` and `e` decode to. `ok(false)` is a signature that
does not verify, including one of the wrong length; `err` is a key out of
bounds (a 2048- to 8192-bit modulus, a 1- to 8-byte exponent) or one
OpenSSL rejects.

```slang
import "crypto";

let r = crypto.rsa_verify_sha256(n, e, to_bytes(header_dot_payload), sig);
let valid = r ?? false;
```

**Hashes, MACs, key derivation.** `sha384`/`sha512` and
`hmac_sha384`/`hmac_sha512` (JWS HS384/HS512) sit beside the SHA-256 ones.
`hkdf_sha256(ikm, salt, info, length)` and `hkdf_sha512` are RFC 5869 HKDF:
use them to derive several keys from one secret, never a bare hash. The
length is 1 to 255 hash lengths. `constant_time_eq(a, b)` compares in
time that depends only on the length: use it for MACs, tokens and anything
else an attacker could probe a byte at a time.

```slang
let enc = crypto.hkdf_sha256(master, salt, b"cookie-encryption", 32);
let mac_ok = crypto.constant_time_eq(crypto.hmac_sha256(k, body), sent_mac);
```

**Authenticated encryption.** `seal(key, plaintext, aad)` encrypts with
AES-256-GCM under a fresh random nonce and returns nonce, ciphertext and
tag in one `bytes`. `open(key, box, aad)` checks and decrypts it. The aad
(associated data, which may be empty) is authenticated but not encrypted:
bind a cookie to its name, a record to its id. Because the caller never
chooses a nonce, it cannot reuse one, the mistake that breaks GCM
outright. A key should seal fewer than 2^32 messages this way, so rotate
it, for example via HKDF with a date in `info`. When a protocol fixes the
nonce, `aes256gcm_seal`/`aes256gcm_open` and
`chacha20poly1305_seal`/`chacha20poly1305_open` take (key, nonce, data,
aad) with a 32-byte key and a 12-byte nonce, and carry ciphertext then a
16-byte tag. Every opener returns an error, never partial plaintext, when
anything was altered.

```slang
let box = crypto.seal(key, to_bytes(session_json), b"session");
let back = crypto.open(key, box ?? b"", b"session");   // err if tampered
```

**Signatures.** Keys use the raw forms JWK and JWS use. Ed25519 has a
32-byte private seed, a 32-byte public key and a 64-byte signature.
ECDSA P-256 with SHA-256 (JWS ES256) has a 32-byte private scalar, a
65-byte uncompressed public point (`0x04 || x || y`) and a 64-byte
`r || s` signature. RSA keys are PEM text.

| | Ed25519 | ECDSA P-256 | RSA (SHA-256) |
|---|---|---|---|
| new key | `ed25519_generate()` | `ecdsa_p256_generate()` | `rsa_generate(bits)` (PEM) |
| public key | `ed25519_public_key(priv)` | `ecdsa_p256_public_key(priv)` | `rsa_public_n(pem)`, `rsa_public_e(pem)` |
| sign | `ed25519_sign(priv, msg)` | `ecdsa_p256_sign_sha256(priv, msg)` | `rsa_sign_sha256(pem, msg)` (RS256), `rsa_sign_pss_sha256` (PS256) |
| verify | `ed25519_verify(pub, msg, sig)` | `ecdsa_p256_verify_sha256(pub, msg, sig)` | `rsa_verify_sha256(n, e, msg, sig)`, `rsa_verify_pss_sha256` |
| from PEM | `ed25519_private_from_pem`, `ed25519_public_from_pem` | `ecdsa_p256_private_from_pem`, `ecdsa_p256_public_from_pem` | (sign takes PEM) |
| to PEM | `ed25519_private_to_pem(priv)` | `ecdsa_p256_private_to_pem(priv)` | (already PEM) |
| encrypt | | | `rsa_encrypt_oaep_sha256(pem, data)`, `rsa_encrypt_oaep_sha1` |
| decrypt | | | `rsa_decrypt_oaep_sha256(pem, data)`, `rsa_decrypt_oaep_sha1` |

Verifiers return `ok(false)` for a signature that does not verify
(including one of the wrong length) and `err` for a malformed key, such
as a P-256 point that is not on the curve. ECDSA signatures are
deterministic (RFC 6979) on OpenSSL 3.2 and newer, so a weak random
number generator cannot leak the key; older 3.x uses random nonces. PSS
fixes the salt at the digest length, as PS256 requires. RSA key
generation takes tens of milliseconds at 2048 bits and seconds at 4096,
without yielding, so do it at startup or in a tool. Prepared keys are
cached (up to 16), so signing or verifying repeatedly with the same keys,
as a server does with its JWT key or a JWKS, skips rebuilding them.
RSA-OAEP encrypts to a public key and decrypts with the private one, the
same hash for the label and MGF1. Use SHA-256 for anything new; SHA-1 is
there for MySQL's password exchange, and OAEP does not depend on the
hash's collision resistance the way a signature does. The `*_to_pem`
functions write a raw private key as PKCS#8 PEM, the form
`net.tls_ctx_use_cert` and `x509` take.

**X.509** lives in the `x509` package; the `crypto.x509_*` functions are
the layer under it (`x509_der`, `x509_fields`, `x509_check_host`,
`x509_verify`, `x509_csr`, `x509_self_signed`), compiled into a program
only when it calls one.

## API

### `crypto.sha256(bytes) -> bytes`

### `crypto.hmac_sha256(bytes, bytes) -> bytes`

### `crypto.rand(int) -> result[bytes,str]`

### `crypto.sha1(bytes) -> bytes`

### `crypto.md5(bytes) -> bytes`

### `crypto.pbkdf2_sha256(bytes, bytes, int, int) -> result[bytes,str]`

### `crypto.argon2id_raw(bytes, bytes, int, int, int, int) -> result[bytes,str]`

### `crypto.argon2id_verify(bytes, bytes, bytes, int, int, int) -> result[bool,str]`

### `crypto.scrypt(bytes, bytes, int, int, int, int) -> result[bytes,str]`

### `crypto.bcrypt_verify(bytes, str) -> result[bool,str]`

### `crypto.rsa_verify_sha256(bytes, bytes, bytes, bytes) -> result[bool,str]`

### `crypto.sha384(bytes) -> bytes`

### `crypto.sha512(bytes) -> bytes`

### `crypto.hmac_sha384(bytes, bytes) -> bytes`

### `crypto.hmac_sha512(bytes, bytes) -> bytes`

### `crypto.hkdf_sha256(bytes, bytes, bytes, int) -> result[bytes,str]`

### `crypto.hkdf_sha512(bytes, bytes, bytes, int) -> result[bytes,str]`

### `crypto.constant_time_eq(bytes, bytes) -> bool`

### `crypto.aes256gcm_seal(bytes, bytes, bytes, bytes) -> result[bytes,str]`

### `crypto.aes256gcm_open(bytes, bytes, bytes, bytes) -> result[bytes,str]`

### `crypto.chacha20poly1305_seal(bytes, bytes, bytes, bytes) -> result[bytes,str]`

### `crypto.chacha20poly1305_open(bytes, bytes, bytes, bytes) -> result[bytes,str]`

### `crypto.seal(bytes, bytes, bytes) -> result[bytes,str]`

### `crypto.open(bytes, bytes, bytes) -> result[bytes,str]`

### `crypto.ed25519_generate() -> result[bytes,str]`

### `crypto.ed25519_public_key(bytes) -> result[bytes,str]`

### `crypto.ed25519_sign(bytes, bytes) -> result[bytes,str]`

### `crypto.ed25519_verify(bytes, bytes, bytes) -> result[bool,str]`

### `crypto.ed25519_private_from_pem(str) -> result[bytes,str]`

### `crypto.ed25519_public_from_pem(str) -> result[bytes,str]`

### `crypto.ed25519_private_to_pem(bytes) -> result[str,str]`

### `crypto.ecdsa_p256_generate() -> result[bytes,str]`

### `crypto.ecdsa_p256_public_key(bytes) -> result[bytes,str]`

### `crypto.ecdsa_p256_sign_sha256(bytes, bytes) -> result[bytes,str]`

### `crypto.ecdsa_p256_verify_sha256(bytes, bytes, bytes) -> result[bool,str]`

### `crypto.ecdsa_p256_private_from_pem(str) -> result[bytes,str]`

### `crypto.ecdsa_p256_public_from_pem(str) -> result[bytes,str]`

### `crypto.ecdsa_p256_private_to_pem(bytes) -> result[str,str]`

### `crypto.rsa_generate(int) -> result[str,str]`

### `crypto.rsa_public_n(str) -> result[bytes,str]`

### `crypto.rsa_public_e(str) -> result[bytes,str]`

### `crypto.rsa_sign_sha256(str, bytes) -> result[bytes,str]`

### `crypto.rsa_sign_pss_sha256(str, bytes) -> result[bytes,str]`

### `crypto.rsa_encrypt_oaep_sha1(str, bytes) -> result[bytes,str]`

### `crypto.rsa_decrypt_oaep_sha1(str, bytes) -> result[bytes,str]`

### `crypto.rsa_encrypt_oaep_sha256(str, bytes) -> result[bytes,str]`

### `crypto.rsa_decrypt_oaep_sha256(str, bytes) -> result[bytes,str]`

### `crypto.rsa_verify_pss_sha256(bytes, bytes, bytes, bytes) -> result[bool,str]`

### `crypto.x509_der(str) -> result[bytes,str]`

### `crypto.x509_fields(bytes) -> result[[str],str]`

### `crypto.x509_check_host(bytes, str) -> bool`

### `crypto.x509_verify(bytes, str, str, int, str) -> result[bool,str]`

### `crypto.x509_csr(str, str, [str]) -> result[str,str]`

### `crypto.x509_self_signed(str, str, [str], int) -> result[str,str]`
