slang is built and maintained by **Dolphlabs** (Dolph Tech Limited) — https://dolphlabs.com



# s3

# s3

> Package s3.

S3-compatible object storage, signed with AWS Signature Version 4: AWS S3,
Cloudflare R2, MinIO and the rest.

```slang
import "s3";
import "proc";

let r = s3.new_client("https://s3.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com", "eu-west-1", access_key, secret_key);
// or s3.from_env(proc.getenv): AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY,
// AWS_SESSION_TOKEN, AWS_REGION, S3_ENDPOINT
guard let c = r else let e = err_of(r) { panic(e); }

s3.put_object(c, "uploads", "avatars/42.png", png, "image/png", deadline);   // ok(etag)
s3.get_object(c, "uploads", "avatars/42.png", deadline);                     // ok(bytes)
s3.get_range(c, "uploads", "logs/today", 0, 1023, deadline);                 // first KiB
s3.head_object(c, "uploads", "avatars/42.png", deadline);                    // ok(some(Object)) or ok(none)
s3.delete_object(c, "uploads", "avatars/42.png", deadline);
s3.list_objects(c, "uploads", "avatars/", "/", "", 1000, deadline);          // ok(Page); page.next continues
s3.put_large(c, "backups", "db.dump", dump, "", 16 * 1048576, deadline);     // multipart
s3.presign_get(c, "uploads", "avatars/42.png", 900);                         // ok(url) for 15 minutes
s3.presign_put(c, "uploads", "incoming/x.bin", 300);
```

The payload is hashed into the signature (`x-amz-content-sha256`), so a
body altered in transit is refused by the server. Signing keys are cached
for the day they belong to. Errors carry S3's own code and message
(`s3: NoSuchKey: The specified key does not exist.`).

**Addressing and listing.** Addressing is path-style by default
(`endpoint/bucket/key`), which MinIO, R2 and most compatible stores want.
Set `c.path_style = false` for virtual-host style (`bucket.endpoint/key`).
`list_objects` returns up to 1000 keys a page in key order. Pass `page.next`
to get the next page; with a delimiter, deeper keys fold into
`page.prefixes`.

**Multipart.** `create_multipart`, `upload_part`, `complete_multipart` and
`abort_multipart` are the raw steps (every part but the last at least
5 MiB). `put_large` drives them, uploading in one request when the data
fits in a part, and aborting if a part fails so no orphaned parts are left
to be billed.

**Presigned URLs** last 1 second to 7 days. `presign_at` signs at a given
time, for tests and for URLs several servers must agree on.

**Google Cloud Storage** speaks the same protocol through its XML API with
HMAC keys (Cloud Storage settings, Interoperability): use
`s3.new_client("https://storage.googleapis.com", "auto", access_id, secret)`.
HMAC keys belong to a service account. For service-account JSON keys or
the metadata server, use the separate `dolphlabs/gcs` package.

## API

### `gc struct Client`

### `gc struct Object`

### `gc struct Page`

### `fn new_client(endpoint: str, region: str, access_key: str, secret_key: str) -> result[Client, str]`

A client for endpoint ("https://s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com", "https://<account>.r2.cloudflarestorage.com", "http://127.0.0.1:9000").

### `fn from_env(getenv: fn(str) -> opt[str]) -> result[Client, str]`

A client from AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, AWS_SESSION_TOKEN (optional), AWS_REGION (or AWS_DEFAULT_REGION) and S3_ENDPOINT (default: the region's AWS endpoint).

### `fn put_object(c: Client, bucket: str, key: str, data: bytes, content_type: str, deadline: until) -> result[str, str]`

Store data at bucket/key; the object's ETag.

### `fn get_object(c: Client, bucket: str, key: str, deadline: until) -> result[bytes, str]`

### `fn get_range(c: Client, bucket: str, key: str, first: int, last: int, deadline: until) -> result[bytes, str]`

Bytes first..last of the object, both included (an HTTP Range).

### `fn head_object(c: Client, bucket: str, key: str, deadline: until) -> result[opt[Object], str]`

Size, ETag, type and modification time, without the body. none when the object does not exist.

### `fn delete_object(c: Client, bucket: str, key: str, deadline: until) -> result[bool, str]`

Delete bucket/key. S3 answers success for a key that was not there.

### `fn list_objects(c: Client, bucket: str, prefix: str, delimiter: str, next: str, max_keys: int, deadline: until) -> result[Page, str]`

One page (up to max_keys, at most 1000) of the keys under prefix, in key order, from where `next` (a Page's next, or "" to start) says. With delimiter "/", keys below the next "/" fold into page.prefixes.

### `fn create_multipart(c: Client, bucket: str, key: str, content_type: str, deadline: until) -> result[str, str]`

Start a multipart upload; its upload id.

### `fn upload_part(c: Client, bucket: str, key: str, upload_id: str, n: int, data: bytes, deadline: until) -> result[str, str]`

Upload part number n (1 to 10000) of an upload; its ETag, for complete_multipart. Every part but the last must be at least 5 MiB.

### `fn complete_multipart(c: Client, bucket: str, key: str, upload_id: str, etags: [str], deadline: until) -> result[str, str]`

Finish an upload from its parts' ETags, in part order; the object's ETag.

### `fn abort_multipart(c: Client, bucket: str, key: str, upload_id: str, deadline: until) -> result[bool, str]`

### `fn put_large(c: Client, bucket: str, key: str, data: bytes, content_type: str, part_size: int, deadline: until) -> result[str, str]`

Upload data in parts of part_size bytes (at least 5 MiB), aborting the upload if any part fails, so no orphaned parts are left to be billed.

### `fn create_bucket(c: Client, bucket: str, deadline: until) -> result[bool, str]`

### `fn delete_bucket(c: Client, bucket: str, deadline: until) -> result[bool, str]`

### `fn presign_get(c: Client, bucket: str, key: str, expires_seconds: int) -> result[str, str]`

A URL anyone can GET (or PUT, below) for expires_seconds (1 second to 7 days), signed now: for downloads and browser uploads that never see your keys.

### `fn presign_put(c: Client, bucket: str, key: str, expires_seconds: int) -> result[str, str]`

### `fn presign_at(c: Client, method: str, bucket: str, key: str, expires_seconds: int, amzdate: str) -> result[str, str]`

presign at a given time ("20130524T000000Z"), for tests and for URLs that must agree across servers.

### `fn sign_request(c: Client, method: str, host: str, path: str, query: map[str]str, headers: map[str]str, payload_hash: str, amzdate: str) -> str`

The Authorization header for a request (SigV4, signed headers are host, x-amz-content-sha256, x-amz-date, any x-amz-security-token and the caller's headers). headers holds lowercase names.

### `fn uri_encode(s: str, keep_slash: bool) -> str`

RFC 3986 percent-encoding as SigV4 wants it (sigv4.uri_encode).

---

slang is built and maintained by **Dolphlabs** (Dolph Tech Limited) — https://dolphlabs.com



# sigv4

# sigv4

> Package sigv4.

AWS Signature Version 4 for any service. `s3` signs with it, and so do
clients for SQS, SNS and the rest.

```slang
import "sigv4";

let s = sigv4.new_signer(access_key, secret_key, "eu-west-1", "sqs");
s.session_token = token;                    // temporary credentials, or leave ""
let h: map[str]str = {};
h["content-type"] = "application/x-amz-json-1.0";
h["x-amz-target"] = "AmazonSQS.SendMessage";
let amzdate = sigv4.amz_date_now();         // "20150830T123600Z"
let auth = sigv4.sign(s, "POST", "sqs.eu-west-1.amazonaws.com", "/", {}, h,
                      sigv4.payload_hash(body), amzdate);
// send Authorization: auth, X-Amz-Date: amzdate, the headers in h, and
// X-Amz-Security-Token when there is a token
let url_query = sigv4.presign(s, "GET", host, "/", {}, 900, amzdate);
```

`sign` signs the given headers plus `host`, `x-amz-date` and any security
token. The signing key is derived once a day per signer and replaced as a
whole, so a request never pairs one day's date with another day's key.
`derive_key`, `authorization` and `presign_query` are the same steps for a
caller that keeps its own key, as `s3` does. `uri_encode` and
`canonical_query` encode the way SigV4 signs. The tests use AWS's published
test-suite vectors.

**Limits.** Objects are read and written whole, in memory (or as one byte
range). Redirects are not followed, since a redirect would change the host
the signature covers.

## API

### `gc struct DayKey { date: str, key: bytes }`

The signing key for one day, held as one object so a request never pairs one day's date with another day's key while the day turns.

### `gc struct Signer`

### `fn new_signer(access_key: str, secret_key: str, region: str, service: str) -> Signer`

### `fn amz_date_now() -> str`

"20130524T000000Z" for now, UTC.

### `fn payload_hash(body: bytes) -> str`

The hex SHA-256 SigV4 signs as the payload hash.

### `fn derive_key(secret_key: str, date: str, region: str, service: str) -> bytes`

kSigning = HMAC(HMAC(HMAC(HMAC("AWS4" + secret, date), region), service), "aws4_request"). `date` is YYYYMMDD.

### `fn signing_key(s: Signer, date: str) -> bytes`

The signer's key for `date`, derived once a day.

### `fn scope(date: str, region: str, service: str) -> str`

### `fn uri_encode(s: str, keep_slash: bool) -> str`

RFC 3986 percent-encoding as SigV4 wants it: everything but A-Z a-z 0-9 - _ . ~ (and / in paths, when keep_slash).

### `fn canonical_query(q: map[str]str) -> str`

Parameters encoded, then sorted by their encoded form: the order SigV4 signs and the order a request should send.

### `fn authorization(access_key: str, key: bytes, region: str, service: str, method: str, path: str, query: map[str]str, headers: map[str]str, payload: str, amzdate: str) -> str`

The Authorization header for a request whose signed headers are exactly `headers` (which must hold host and x-amz-date, and x-amz-security-token with temporary credentials). For callers that keep their own key cache, as s3 does; most callers want `sign`.

### `fn sign(s: Signer, method: str, host: str, path: str, query: map[str]str, headers: map[str]str, payload: str, amzdate: str) -> str`

The Authorization header for a request to `host`: signs `headers` plus host, x-amz-date and, with temporary credentials, x-amz-security-token. The caller sends X-Amz-Date (and the token) with the same values.

### `fn presign_query(access_key: str, key: bytes, region: str, service: str, session_token: str, method: str, host: str, path: str, query: map[str]str, expires_seconds: int, payload: str, amzdate: str) -> str`

The query string of a presigned URL (with X-Amz-Signature last), for a request that signs only the host header. `query` holds the request's own parameters; payload is usually "UNSIGNED-PAYLOAD". For callers with their own key cache; most callers want `presign`.

### `fn presign(s: Signer, method: str, host: str, path: str, query: map[str]str, expires_seconds: int, amzdate: str) -> str`

---

slang is built and maintained by **Dolphlabs** (Dolph Tech Limited) — https://dolphlabs.com



# sort

# sort

> Package sort.

Sorting lists in place with Go's `sort` engine shape, plus binary
search over what is already sorted. `ints`, `floats` and `strings`
sort by native comparison; `by` sorts any list of anything by a key
function returning `int`, `float` or `str`; `by_stable` keeps equal
keys in their original order; the `search` functions binary-search a
sorted list and answer `opt[int]`.

```slang
import "sort";

let xs = [5, 3, 9, 1, 3];
sort.ints(xs);                       // in place, ascending
let i = sort.search_ints(xs, 3) ?? -1;

let users = load_users();
sort.by(users, user_age);            // key fn -> int, float or str
sort.by_stable(users, user_name);    // equal keys keep original order

let names: [str] = [];
for u in users { push(names, u.name); }
sort.strings(names);

let fs = [3.5, 1.0, 0.0 / 0.0, 0.5];
sort.floats(fs);                     // NaN values sort first (Go's rule)
```

The unstable sorts allocate nothing; each runs an entry pass that
answers already-sorted and fully-reversed lists in one scan, and the
quicksort settles each duplicate group in one partition pass, so
four-valued million-element lists sort in tens of milliseconds.
`by_stable` merges with one scratch list of about n/2 elements.

## API

### `fn ints(xs: [int]) -> [int]`

Sorts xs in place, ascending. Unstable. Answers an already-sorted or strictly descending list in one scan, and duplicate-heavy data in no more passes than its distinct values take to settle, so the whole call is allocation-free either way.

### `fn floats(xs: [float]) -> [float]`

Same engine over floats, with a total order despite the type's own: NaN values sort before every number and equal to each other (Go's `sort.Float64s` rule), which is what makes the partition finite.

### `fn strings(xs: [str]) -> [str]`

Same engine over strings, bytewise: `""` sorts first, and the order is exactly what `<` gives — bytes, not locale, not Unicode points.

### `fn by[T, K](xs: [T], key: fn(T) -> K) -> [T]`

Sorts xs in place by key, ascending. Unstable: when two keys are equal, which was first is whatever the comparisons fell into. A call is free to permute equal keys differently on a re-run, so anything whose output must not change between runs uses `by_stable`.

### `fn by_stable[T, K](xs: [T], key: fn(T) -> K) -> [T]`

Sorts xs in place by key, ascending, and equal keys keep their original order: an adaptive merge sort. Natural runs are kept (a strictly descending run is reversed, which keeps order for equal keys, since a strictly descending run has none), windows of 32 are insertion-sorted, and runs merge bottom-up taking the left on equal keys. Nearly-sorted data therefore costs about one comparison per element, not n log n.

### `fn search_ints(xs: [int], v: int) -> opt[int]`

The first index of v in xs, sorted ascending, or none. On a list which is not sorted the result is defined but useless; it never reads past the list.

### `fn search_floats(xs: [float], v: float) -> opt[int]`

Same contract over floats: that includes searching for NaN, which finds the first NaN and sorts first under sort.floats. The index found for a searched NaN is where the first NaN of the list sits.

### `fn search_strings(xs: [str], v: str) -> opt[int]`

Same contract over strings: the first index of an exactly equal string, bytewise as `sort.strings` orders them.

### `fn search_by[T, K](xs: [T], key: fn(T) -> K, v: K) -> opt[int]`

Lower bound over a list already sorted by key: the first index whose key is not before v. Equality is `!(a < b) && !(b < a)`, which is `==` for int and str keys; for a float key it reads equal NaNs -- both raw comparisons false -- as a hit, the same reading `by` gives them.

---

slang is built and maintained by **Dolphlabs** (Dolph Tech Limited) — https://dolphlabs.com



# sql

# sql

> Package sql.

A SQLite driver (linked automatically, only when a program imports
`sql`). Connections and prepared statements are opaque `rawptr`
handles, exactly like `net.tls_*`; free them with `sql.close` /
`sql.finalize`. **Every fallible call returns `result[_, str]` whose
error is SQLite's own message** — `no such table: users`, `near
"SELCT": syntax error`, `UNIQUE constraint failed: users.id` — so a
bad query stays as visible as a bad socket read (`guard let … else
let e = err_of(r)`), never a silent `null`. The column getters are
infallible (SQLite coerces types; an out-of-range index is a
programming error, returning `0` / `""`), so they return bare values.

| Function | Signature |
|----------|-----------|
| `sql.open(path)` | `result[rawptr, str]` — `":memory:"` for in-memory |
| `sql.close(db)` | — |
| `sql.exec(db, sql)` | `result[int, str]` — runs statement(s), returns rows changed |
| `sql.last_insert_id(db)` | `int` |
| `sql.prepare(db, sql)` | `result[rawptr, str]` |
| `sql.finalize(st)` | — |
| `sql.reset(st)` | `result[bool, str]` — clears bindings, re-run |
| `sql.bind_int/bind_float/bind_text/bind_blob(st, idx, v)` | `result[bool, str]` — `idx` is 1-based |
| `sql.bind_null(st, idx)` | `result[bool, str]` |
| `sql.step(st)` | `result[bool, str]` — `true` = row ready, `false` = done |
| `sql.col_count(st)` | `int` |
| `sql.col_name(st, i)` / `col_text(st, i)` | `str` — `i` is 0-based |
| `sql.col_int(st, i)` | `int` |
| `sql.col_float(st, i)` | `float` |
| `sql.col_blob(st, i)` | `bytes` |
| `sql.col_is_null(st, i)` | `bool` |

```slang
import "sql";
import "log";

let dr = sql.open("app.db");
guard let db = dr else let e = err_of(dr) {
    log.error("db open: " + e);
    exit(1);
}
sql.exec(db, "CREATE TABLE users (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT)");

let pr = sql.prepare(db, "SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE id > ?");
guard let st = pr else let e = err_of(pr) {
    log.error("prepare: " + e);          // e.g. "no such table: users"
    exit(1);
}
sql.bind_int(st, 1, 0);
while true {
    let sr = sql.step(st);
    guard let more = sr else let e = err_of(sr) { log.error("step: " + e); break; }
    if !more { break; }
    println(to_str(sql.col_int(st, 0)) + " " + sql.col_text(st, 1));
}
sql.finalize(st);
sql.close(db);
```

SQLite calls block the worker — use them for real work off the accept
loop (wrap in a `spawn`ed task), the same caveat as `fs`. One
connection per `rawptr`; there is no pool and no async stepping. For
Postgres, see [`pg`](#pg), which runs on the scheduler instead.

Query complexity is capped per connection so SQLite's recursion stays
inside the task stack: at most **50 terms in a compound `SELECT`**
(`UNION`/`INTERSECT`/`EXCEPT`) and an **expression depth of 400**
(roughly, terms in one `AND`/`OR` chain). SQLite's stock limits of 500
and 1000 allow a single legal query to want ~325KB of C stack, which
would force a task stack far too fat to spawn per connection. Long
`IN` lists, wide result sets, and recursive CTEs are *not* affected —
they don't recurse. Exceeding a cap is a normal error through
`result[_, str]` (`too many terms in compound SELECT`), not a crash.

## API

### `sql.open(str) -> result[rawptr,str]`

### `sql.close(rawptr)`

### `sql.exec(rawptr, str) -> result[int,str]`

### `sql.last_insert_id(rawptr) -> int`

### `sql.prepare(rawptr, str) -> result[rawptr,str]`

### `sql.finalize(rawptr)`

### `sql.reset(rawptr) -> result[bool,str]`

### `sql.bind_int(rawptr, int, int) -> result[bool,str]`

### `sql.bind_float(rawptr, int, float) -> result[bool,str]`

### `sql.bind_text(rawptr, int, str) -> result[bool,str]`

### `sql.bind_blob(rawptr, int, bytes) -> result[bool,str]`

### `sql.bind_null(rawptr, int) -> result[bool,str]`

### `sql.step(rawptr) -> result[bool,str]`

### `sql.col_count(rawptr) -> int`

### `sql.col_name(rawptr, int) -> str`

### `sql.col_is_null(rawptr, int) -> bool`

### `sql.col_int(rawptr, int) -> int`

### `sql.col_float(rawptr, int) -> float`

### `sql.col_text(rawptr, int) -> str`

### `sql.col_blob(rawptr, int) -> bytes`

---

slang is built and maintained by **Dolphlabs** (Dolph Tech Limited) — https://dolphlabs.com



# strings

# strings

> Package strings.

Search, trim, case, split and join on `str`. The package cannot be named
`str` because that token is the type — the same reason Go calls its own
`strings`.

```slang
import "strings";

strings.find("hello world", "world");   // 6, or -1
strings.rfind("a/b/c", "/");            // 3
strings.contains("hello", "ell");
strings.has_prefix("hello", "he");
strings.has_suffix("hello", "lo");
strings.count("a,b,c", ",");            // 2
strings.hash("user:42");                // a 64-bit hash, never negative: in-process only

strings.trim("  hi \r\n");              // "hi" (space/tab/CR/LF)
strings.trim_start(s); strings.trim_end(s);
strings.to_upper("hi"); strings.to_lower("HI");   // ASCII only

strings.slice("hello", 1, 3);           // "el"
strings.slice("hello", -3, 5);          // "llo" — negative counts back
strings.repeat("ab", 3);                // "ababab"
strings.replace("a,b,c", ",", " | ");

strings.split("a,b,,c", ",");           // ["a", "b", "", "c"]
strings.join(parts, ",");               // the inverse of split
strings.join_bytes(parts, b",");        // the same for [bytes]: sized once, copied once

strings.from_float(0.1 + 0.2);          // "0.30000000000000004"

strings.escape_html("<a href='x'>");    // "&lt;a href=&#39;x&#39;&gt;"
strings.escape_js("it's </script>");    // "it\u0027s \u003c/script\u003e"
```

`escape_html` writes `& < > " '` as character references, which is safe
in text and in a quoted attribute of either quote. `escape_js` makes the
inside of a JavaScript string literal of any quote (`'`, `"` or a
backquote), safe inside `<script>` and inside an attribute. Both return
the input itself, with no allocation, when nothing needs escaping.
`template` escapes every value through them.

`from_float` returns the shortest text that `to_float` reads back as
exactly the same number, as `to_str`, `println`, `inspect` and
`json.encode` now do too (they used six significant digits, so
`to_str(123456789.125)` was `"1.23457e+08"`). The difference is the
names: `from_float` writes NaN and the infinities as `NaN`, `Infinity`
and `-Infinity`, where `to_str` writes `nan`, `inf` and `-inf`.

This is a compiler-provided native package, and it has to be: `str`
supports `len`, `+` and `==` and nothing else — it cannot be indexed or
sliced — so none of it could be written in slang without converting to
`bytes` and back on every call. `byteutil` covers the `bytes` side.

Three behaviours worth knowing:

- **Indices are byte offsets and the case operations are ASCII-only.**
  `str` is UTF-8 bytes, and these are byte operations, which is what
  protocol text (header names, methods, config keys) wants. For text
  people type, use `unicode`: characters, case folding and
  normalisation.
- **`slice` clamps rather than panics.** Slicing is how you narrow a
  string you just searched, and a `find` that returned -1 on the line
  above should not turn the next line into a crash. A negative index
  counts from the end.
- **`split` and `join` are exact inverses.** Adjacent separators produce
  empty elements, so the result always has `count(s, sep) + 1` elements
  and `join(split(s, sep), sep) == s` for any non-empty separator. An
  empty separator splits into single bytes.

## API

### `strings.find(str, str) -> int`

### `strings.rfind(str, str) -> int`

### `strings.contains(str, str) -> bool`

### `strings.has_prefix(str, str) -> bool`

### `strings.has_suffix(str, str) -> bool`

### `strings.count(str, str) -> int`

### `strings.hash(str) -> int`

### `strings.trim(str) -> str`

### `strings.trim_start(str) -> str`

### `strings.trim_end(str) -> str`

### `strings.to_upper(str) -> str`

### `strings.to_lower(str) -> str`

### `strings.slice(str, int, int) -> str`

### `strings.repeat(str, int) -> str`

### `strings.replace(str, str, str) -> str`

### `strings.split(str, str) -> [str]`

### `strings.join([str], str) -> str`

### `strings.join_bytes([bytes], bytes) -> bytes`

### `strings.bytes_zero(int) -> bytes`

### `strings.copy_into(bytes, int, bytes, int, int) -> int`

### `strings.from_bytes(bytes, int, int) -> str`

### `strings.from_bytes_lower(bytes, int, int) -> str`

### `strings.from_wire(wire, int, int) -> str`

### `strings.from_wire_lower(wire, int, int) -> str`

### `strings.find_field(bytes, str) -> int`

### `strings.from_float(float) -> str`

### `strings.escape_html(str) -> str`

### `strings.escape_js(str) -> str`

---

slang is built and maintained by **Dolphlabs** (Dolph Tech Limited) — https://dolphlabs.com



# tar

# tar

> Package tar.

Archives in memory: read every entry of a zip (stored or deflated, ZIP64,
UTF-8 names) or a tar (ustar, pax, GNU long names; a `.tar.gz` is
`compress.gunzip` first), and write either.

```slang
import "tar";
import "zip";

let r = zip.open(data);
guard let arc = r else let e = err_of(r) { panic(e); }
for e in arc.entries {
    let pr = zip.safe_path(e.name);          // refuses ../, /abs, C:\ (zip slip)
    guard let rel = pr else { continue; }
    if !e.is_dir {
        let body = zip.read(arc, e);         // inflated, size and CRC-32 checked
    }
}

let w = zip.new_writer();
w.add("report.csv", csv_bytes, now_unix);    // deflated, or stored if that is smaller
w.add_stored("logo.png", png, now_unix);
let out = w.finish();                        // result[bytes, str]

let tr = tar.parse(tar_bytes);               // result[[tar.Entry], str]
let tw = tar.new_writer();
tw.add_file("bin/run.sh", script, 493, now_unix);    // mode 0755
tw.add_symlink("current", "releases/42", now_unix);
let tb = tw.finish();
```

**Reading is checked against the archive itself.** A zip is read from its
central directory, as unzip does. Each entry's local header must be where
the directory says, its data inside the archive, and no two entries may
share bytes: overlapping entries are how a 40 KB zip claims petabytes.
An entry inflates to at most the size the directory states, and must
match it and its CRC-32. `zip.Limits` bounds one entry (256 MiB), all of
them together (1 GiB) and their count. Every tar header's checksum is
checked, and a size may be octal or GNU base-256. A pax header's `path`,
`linkpath`, `size`, `mtime`, `uid` and `gid` override the ustar fields.
Data past the end of the archive is an error, never a short entry.
Encrypted zip entries and methods other than stored and deflate are
listed but not read. Zip names must be UTF-8, so CP437 names are refused.

**Names are never trusted.** Neither package touches the file system.
`safe_path` gives back a relative, cleaned name, or an error for an
absolute path, a `..` segment, a drive letter, a backslash or a NUL.
Check a tar symlink's target the same way before creating it. Writers
refuse such names, and the same name twice.

**Times** are Unix seconds. A zip's MS-DOS timestamp has no zone and
2-second steps; it is read as UTC, and the extended timestamp extra field
wins when present. `tests/archive_interop` reads archives made by
Python's `zipfile` and `tarfile`, Info-ZIP and bsdtar. What these writers
write was checked with `unzip -t`, Python and bsdtar.

## API

### `gc struct Entry`

### `struct Limits`

### `fn default_limits() -> Limits`

### `fn parse(data: bytes) -> result[[Entry], str]`

### `fn parse_with(data: bytes, lim: Limits) -> result[[Entry], str]`

### `fn safe_path(name: str) -> result[str, str]`

A name made safe to join under an extraction directory: relative, with no "..", no drive letter or backslash, no NUL. A trailing "/" is kept. Check a symlink's target the same way before creating it.

### `gc struct Writer`

### `fn new_writer() -> Writer`

### `fn add_file(self: Writer, name: str, data: bytes, mode: int, modified: int) -> Writer`

### `fn add_dir(self: Writer, name: str, mode: int, modified: int) -> Writer`

### `fn add_symlink(self: Writer, name: str, target: str, modified: int) -> Writer`

### `fn finish(self: Writer) -> result[bytes, str]`

The archive, closed with two zero blocks, or the first problem an add ran into.

---

slang is built and maintained by **Dolphlabs** (Dolph Tech Limited) — https://dolphlabs.com



# template

# template

> Package template.

HTML templates that escape each value for where it lands, and plain-text
templates for email bodies and other text. The syntax is Go's
(`{{ .field }}`, `if`, `range`, `with`, `define`, pipelines), and so is the
safety model: escaping is decided by the HTML around each action when the
template is parsed, not by the caller remembering to escape.

```slang
import "template";

gc struct Item { name: str, url: str, price: int }
gc struct Page { title: str, items: [Item], user: str }

let r = template.parse("page",
    "<h1>{{ .title }}</h1>" +
    "<ul>{{ range $i, $it := .items }}" +
    "<li><a href=\"{{ $it.url }}\" title=\"{{ $it.name }}\">{{ add $i 1 }}. {{ $it.name }}</a></li>" +
    "{{ else }}<li>nothing yet</li>{{ end }}</ul>" +
    "<script>const user = {{ .user }};</script>");
guard let t = r else let e = err_of(r) { panic(e); }      // syntax and context errors, with line numbers
let html = template.render(t, page);                       // result[str, str]

template.add(t, "layout", "<html><body>{{ template \"page\" . }}</body></html>");
template.render_named(t, "layout", page);

let mail = template.parse_text("welcome", "Hi {{ .name }},\n{{ range .items }}- {{ .name }}\n{{ end }}");
```

Each action is escaped for its context:

| Where | What the value becomes |
|---|---|
| text, quoted attribute | `& < > " '` as character references |
| URL attribute (`href`, `src`, `action`, …), at the start | only `http`, `https`, `mailto`, `tel` or a relative URL; anything else, `javascript:` above all, becomes `about:invalid#blocked` |
| later in a URL | percent-encoded (`/search?q={{ .q }}`) |
| `<script>`, `on*` attributes | a JavaScript literal (JSON), `<` `>` `&` `'` as `\u` escapes |
| inside a JS string | escaped as string content, whatever the quotes |
| `<style>`, `style` attributes | letters, digits and `# % . , -` only, else `ZgotmplZ` |

Refused when the template is parsed: an action in a tag or attribute
name, in an unquoted attribute value, in an HTML or JavaScript comment,
and branches of an `if` or `range` that leave the HTML in different
states (`{{ if .x }}<a href="{{ end }}`). `{{ .html | raw }}` writes
trusted HTML unescaped in text, and escapes it anywhere else.

**Data** is any value `json.encode` takes: a struct's fields are `.name`,
a list ranges, a map's keys are fields (ranged in sorted key order).
A missing field is an error, not an empty string, so a typo does not
render as silence; use `if`, `with` or `default` for data that may be
absent.

**Language.** `{{ if }}`/`{{ else if }}`/`{{ else }}`, `{{ with }}`,
`{{ range }}` (with `$i, $x :=` and `{{ else }}` for empty), `{{ $x := … }}`
and `{{ $x = … }}` with block scope, `$` for the root, pipelines
(`{{ .name | upper }}`), parentheses (`{{ len (index .items 0).tags }}`),
`{{/* comments */}}` and `{{-`/`-}}` to trim whitespace, `{{ define }}`
and `{{ template "name" . }}` (nested up to 64 deep). Functions: `eq ne
lt le gt ge`, `and or not` (short-circuit, as Go's), `len index default
join upper lower trim add sub`, `print printf` (`%s %v %d %f %.2f %q %x
%t`), `json urlquery raw`. An unknown function or variable is a parse
error.

**Cost.** Parsing and escape analysis happen once; a `Template` is safe
to render from many tasks at once. Rendering encodes the data with
`json.encode` and indexes it with `encoding.json_tape` (one C pass, no
allocation per value), resolves variables to slots at parse time, and
escapes with `strings.escape_html`/`escape_js`, which return their input
unchanged when nothing needs escaping. A 100-row table page (15 KB, six
actions a row) rendered in 0.6–0.8 ms, against 1.0–1.2 ms for Go's
`html/template` on the same page, run alternately on one machine.

## API

### `gc struct Template`

A set of named templates, parsed and ready to render: make one with parse or parse_text, grow it with add. Its fields are internal. Safe to render from many tasks at once.

### `fn parse(name: str, src: str) -> result[Template, str]`

An HTML template, escaped by context. src may hold {{ define }} blocks.

### `fn parse_text(name: str, src: str) -> result[Template, str]`

A plain-text template (email bodies, CLI output): nothing is escaped.

### `fn add(t: Template, name: str, src: str) -> result[bool, str]`

Add another named template, such as a partial or a layout, which any template in the set can call with {{ template "name" }} (passing dot, or the value written after the name); its {{ define }} blocks are added too.

### `fn render[T](t: Template, data: T) -> result[str, str]`

Render the template parse was given, with data as its dot.

### `fn render_named[T](t: Template, name: str, data: T) -> result[str, str]`

Render one of the templates (a define or one added with add).

### `fn escape_html(s: str) -> str`

HTML-escape text, for building markup by hand.

---

slang is built and maintained by **Dolphlabs** (Dolph Tech Limited) — https://dolphlabs.com



# time

# time

> Package time.

```slang
import "time";

let t0 = time.mono();     // monotonic clock; a `duration` (int64 ns)
time.sleep(20000000);     // sleep for a duration (ns)
let elapsed = time.mono() - t0;   // duration arithmetic
let deadline = time.mono() + 5000000;  // timeout math for net calls

let wall = time.wall();   // unix epoch time in nanoseconds
let d = time.http_date(); // "Tue, 13 Oct 2026 09:30:15 GMT", the current second
```

`time.put_http_date(w, off)` writes the same 29 bytes into a `wire` and
returns `off + 29` (with a zero-length wire it only counts): what `http`
uses for `Date`. For dates other than now, use `timez`.

## API

### `time.mono() -> duration`

### `time.wall() -> int`

### `time.sleep(int)`

### `time.http_date() -> str`

### `time.put_http_date(wire, int) -> int`

---

slang is built and maintained by **Dolphlabs** (Dolph Tech Limited) — https://dolphlabs.com



# timez

# timez

> Package timez.

Calendar time, written in slang on top of the native `time` clock:
instants, dates, durations, text formats, time zones, test clocks and
cron. Import `"timez"`.

```slang
import "timez";

let t = timez.now();                               // a Time: an instant, UTC
println(t.rfc3339());                              // 2026-10-13T09:30:15Z
println(t.rfc3339_milli());                        // 2026-10-13T09:30:15.000Z (toISOString)
println(t.http_date());                            // Tue, 13 Oct 2026 09:30:15 GMT
println(t.format("%A %e %B %Y, %H:%M"));          // Tuesday 13 October 2026, 09:30

let r = timez.parse_rfc3339("2026-10-13T11:30:15+02:00");   // offsets applied
let due = t.date().add_months(1);                  // Jan 31 + 1 month = Feb 28/29
let ttl = timez.parse_duration("1h30m") ?? 0;      // nanoseconds; "7d" works too
println(timez.relative(t.add(-3 * timez.MINUTE), t));  // 3 minutes ago

let zr = timez.load_zone("Europe/Berlin");         // the system's tz database
guard let berlin = zr else let e = err_of(zr) { println(e); exit(1); }
println(t.in_zone(berlin).format("%H:%M %Z"));     // 11:30 CEST

let cr = timez.parse_cron("*/15 9-17 * * MON-FRI");
guard let cron = cr else let e = err_of(cr) { println(e); exit(1); }
let next = cron.next_after(t, berlin);             // opt[Time], DST-aware
```

**Values.**
- **`Time`** is Unix seconds plus nanoseconds, so it spans 0001-01-01 to
  9999-12-31 and beyond. 64-bit nanoseconds stop at 1677-2262.
- **`Date`** is a calendar day: birthdays, due dates, report days.
- **Durations** are `int` nanoseconds, the unit `time.sleep` and deadlines
  take. Constants run from `NANOSECOND` to `HOUR` and `DAY` (24 hours).
- **The calendar** is proleptic Gregorian, with no leap seconds.

**Calendar.**
- Fields: `year()` to `nanosecond()`, `weekday()`, `year_day()`,
  `iso_week()`, `is_leap_year`, `days_in_month`.
- Arithmetic: `add(d)`, `sub(t)`, and `add_days`, `add_months` and
  `add_years`, which clamp to the end of the month.
- Rounding and periods: `truncate(d)`, `round(d)`, and `start_of_*` and
  `end_of_*` for minute, hour, day, week (Monday), month and year.
- Comparing: `before`, `after`, `equal`, `compare`, `min`, `max`.
- Dates: `days_until`, and `years_until`, which counts an age by whether
  the anniversary has passed.

**Text.**
- `rfc3339`, `rfc3339_milli`, `rfc3339_nano` and `rfc3339_at(offset)`.
- `parse_rfc3339` is strict: it refuses a timestamp with no offset,
  because one without names no instant.
- `parse_date`.
- `http_date`, and `parse_http_date` for all three forms RFC 9110 has
  recipients accept.
- `rfc2822` and `parse_rfc2822`.
- `format(layout)`: `strftime` directives, locale-free.
- `parse_duration` and `format_duration`, Go's format plus `d`.
- `relative`.

**Time zones.**
- **Loading.** `load_zone(name)` reads the IANA database, from `$ZONEINFO`
  or `/usr/share/zoneinfo`. It follows each file's POSIX-TZ rule past its
  last transition, and refuses names that could reach other files. A
  missing database is an error that says how to install it, never a
  silent UTC. `fixed_zone(name, offset)` gives a zone at a fixed offset.
- **Reading.** `t.in_zone(z)` gives a `ZonedTime`: local fields, `abbrev`,
  `is_dst`, `rfc3339` with the offset, and `format` with real `%z` and `%Z`.
- **Local arithmetic.** `add_days`, `add_months` and `start_of_day` work in
  local wall time, so a day across a DST change is 23 or 25 hours.
- **Wall time to instant.** `zoned(z, y, m, d, h, mi, s, how)` converts a
  local wall time to an instant. `how` decides the skipped and repeated
  hours: `COMPATIBLE` moves forward through a gap and takes the earlier of
  an overlap, as Temporal and java.time do. The others are `EARLIER`,
  `LATER` and `REJECT`.

**Operations.**
- `system_clock()` / `fixed_clock(t)`: a `Clock` to pass in state, so
  tests `advance` and `set` the time instead of sleeping.
- `start_stopwatch()`, which measures on the monotonic clock.
- `interval(a, b)`: half-open, with `contains`, `overlaps` and
  `intersection`.
- `deadline(t)` gives the `until` that socket and channel calls take.
- **`parse_cron`:** five fields, names, steps and `@daily` macros. When
  both day fields are set, a day matches either (Vixie). `next_after(t,
  zone)` evaluates in the zone's wall time: a run in a skipped hour
  happens when the clock reaches it, and a repeated hour runs once.


**In JSON and Postgres.** A `timez.Time` field of a struct is written by
`json.encode` as an RFC 3339 string and read back by `json.decode` (see
`json`). `pg.arg_time(t)` binds one for a `timestamptz` parameter and
`pg.get_time(rows, r, c)` reads one out; `pg.timestamp_rfc3339(cell,
has_tz)` turns Postgres's own timestamp text into RFC 3339.

## API

### `fn rfc3339(self: Time) -> str`

"2026-10-13T09:30:15Z": seconds, UTC.

### `fn rfc3339_milli(self: Time) -> str`

"2026-10-13T09:30:15.000Z": always milliseconds, as JavaScript's toISOString() writes them -- what a browser client parses most happily.

### `fn rfc3339_nano(self: Time) -> str`

"2026-10-13T09:30:15.5Z": every nanosecond the instant has, no trailing zeros -- what round-trips exactly.

### `fn rfc3339_at(self: Time, offset_seconds: int) -> str`

The same instant as the wall time at a fixed offset from UTC (seconds east, -64800 to 64800): "2026-10-13T11:30:15+02:00".

### `fn http_date(self: Time) -> str`

"Tue, 13 Oct 2026 09:30:15 GMT": the HTTP date (RFC 9110 IMF-fixdate) for Date, Last-Modified, Expires and cookie Expires.

### `fn rfc2822(self: Time) -> str`

"Tue, 13 Oct 2026 09:30:15 +0000": email (RFC 5322) dates.

### `fn format(self: Time, layout: str) -> str`

strftime-style formatting, locale-free (English names), UTC:  %Y year (2026)   %m month 01-12   %d day 01-31   %e day, space-padded %H hour 00-23    %I hour 01-12    %M minute      %S second    %p AM/PM %L milliseconds (000-999)   %f microseconds   %N nanoseconds (9 digits) %a Tue  %A Tuesday  %b Oct  %B October  %j day of year 001-366 %u weekday 1-7 (Monday 1)  %G ISO year  %V ISO week 01-53 %s Unix seconds   %z +0000   %Z UTC   %F %Y-%m-%d   %T %H:%M:%S   %% %  An unknown directive is written as it is, so a typo shows in the output instead of vanishing.

### `fn parse_date(s: str) -> result[Date, str]`

"2026-10-13" (and only that): a calendar date.

### `fn parse_rfc3339(s: str) -> result[Time, str]`

An RFC 3339 timestamp: "2026-10-13T09:30:15Z", with an optional fraction of up to 9 digits and a "Z" or "+hh:mm"/"-hh:mm" offset, which is applied: the result is the instant, in UTC. "t" and "z" and a space for "T" are accepted, as RFC 3339 allows. A missing offset is refused: a timestamp without one names no instant.

### `fn parse_http_date(s: str) -> result[Time, str]`

An HTTP date. RFC 9110 has recipients accept three forms, and so does this:  Tue, 13 Oct 2026 09:30:15 GMT       IMF-fixdate (what everything sends) Tuesday, 13-Oct-26 09:30:15 GMT     RFC 850 (two-digit year: more than 50 years ahead means last century) Tue Oct 13 09:30:15 2026            asctime

### `fn parse_rfc2822(s: str) -> result[Time, str]`

An email date (RFC 5322): an optional weekday, a 1-2 digit day, a month, a 4-digit year, hh:mm with optional :ss, and a "+hhmm"/"-hhmm" offset or UT/GMT/Z.

### `fn relative(t: Time, now_t: Time) -> str`

How long ago `t` was, or how far ahead, from `now_t`, the way people say it: "just now", "45 seconds ago", "3 minutes ago", "in 2 hours", "yesterday", "5 days ago", "in 3 weeks", "2 months ago", "1 year ago". Rounded down, so "1 hour ago" means at least an hour.

### `gc struct Clock`

Where code gets the time, so a test can set it instead of sleeping. Pass a Clock in your state; production uses system_clock().

### `fn system_clock() -> Clock`

### `fn fixed_clock(t: Time) -> Clock`

A clock that stays at `t` until advanced or set.

### `fn now(self: Clock) -> Time`

### `fn advance(self: Clock, d: int) -> Time`

Moves a fixed clock forward by `d` (no effect on the system clock).

### `fn set(self: Clock, t: Time)`

### `struct Stopwatch`

Measures elapsed time on the monotonic clock: a wall-clock correction (NTP, a person setting the time) cannot make it jump or go backwards.

### `fn start_stopwatch() -> Stopwatch`

### `fn elapsed(self: Stopwatch) -> int`

Nanoseconds since the stopwatch started.

### `fn elapsed_text(self: Stopwatch) -> str`

"1.502s".

### `struct Interval`

A half-open span [start, end): it contains its start, not its end, so back-to-back intervals (09:00-10:00, 10:00-11:00) do not overlap.

### `fn interval(start: Time, end: Time) -> result[Interval, str]`

err when `end` is before `start`.

### `fn contains(self: Interval, t: Time) -> bool`

### `fn overlaps(self: Interval, o: Interval) -> bool`

### `fn intersection(self: Interval, o: Interval) -> opt[Interval]`

The span both cover, none when they do not overlap.

### `fn length(self: Interval) -> int`

Nanoseconds from start to end.

### `fn is_empty(self: Interval) -> bool`

### `gc struct Cron`

A five-field cron schedule: minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week. Each field takes `*`, numbers, ranges (`9-17`), lists (`1,15`), steps (`*/15`, `0-30/10`), month names (JAN-DEC) and weekday names (SUN-SAT; 0 and 7 are both Sunday). Macros: @yearly @annually @monthly @weekly @daily @midnight @hourly. As in Vixie cron, when both day fields are restricted a day matches either one.

### `fn parse_cron(spec: str) -> result[Cron, str]`

### `fn next_after(self: Cron, t: Time, z: Zone) -> opt[Time]`

The first run strictly after `t`, read on the clocks of `z`; none when the schedule never matches (Feb 30) within eight years. A run whose wall time a daylight-saving change skips happens when the clock reaches it (moved forward); one the change repeats runs once.

### `let NANOSECOND = 1;`

### `let MICROSECOND = 1000;`

### `let MILLISECOND = 1000000;`

### `let SECOND = 1000000000;`

### `let MINUTE = 60000000000;`

### `let HOUR = 3600000000000;`

### `let DAY = 86400000000000;`

24 hours.

### `struct Time`

An instant, in UTC.

### `struct Date`

A calendar day, with no time and no zone: a birthday, a due date, a day of a report.

### `struct IsoWeek`

An ISO 8601 week: weeks start on Monday, and week 1 is the one with the year's first Thursday, so early January can belong to the previous year's last week.

### `fn days_from_civil(y: int, m: int, d: int) -> int`

Days since 1970-01-01 for a civil date (Howard Hinnant's algorithm: exact for every proleptic Gregorian date in range).

### `fn civil_from_days(days: int) -> Date`

The civil date `days` after 1970-01-01.

### `fn is_leap_year(y: int) -> bool`

### `fn days_in_month(y: int, m: int) -> int`

### `fn days_in_year(y: int) -> int`

### `fn weekday_index(w: Weekday) -> int`

Monday 0 through Sunday 6.

### `fn weekday_name(w: Weekday) -> str`

"Monday" ... "Sunday".

### `fn month_name(m: int) -> str`

"January" ... "December"; "" outside 1-12.

### `fn now() -> Time`

The current instant, from the system clock.

### `fn unix(sec: int) -> Time`

### `fn unix_milli(ms: int) -> Time`

### `fn unix_nano(ns: int) -> Time`

### `fn utc(year: int, month: int, day: int, hour: int, minute: int, second: int, nanos: int) -> result[Time, str]`

The instant at a UTC civil date and time; err names the first field out of range. Seconds run 0-59: there are no leap seconds.

### `fn date(year: int, month: int, day: int) -> result[Date, str]`

A calendar date; err names what is out of range.

### `fn today() -> Date`

Today's date, in UTC.

### `fn min(a: Time, b: Time) -> Time`

### `fn max(a: Time, b: Time) -> Time`

### `fn since(t: Time) -> int`

Nanoseconds since `t` (negative when `t` is in the future).

### `fn until(t: Time) -> int`

Nanoseconds until `t` (negative when it has passed).

### `fn deadline(t: Time) -> until`

The `until` a socket or channel call takes, for the wall-clock instant `t`: deadlines run on the monotonic clock, so this measures the distance to `t` once and counts it from now.

### `fn unix(self: Time) -> int`

### `fn unix_milli(self: Time) -> int`

### `fn unix_nano(self: Time) -> int`

Nanoseconds since the epoch; saturates outside 1677-2262.

### `fn date(self: Time) -> Date`

### `fn year(self: Time) -> int`

### `fn month(self: Time) -> int`

### `fn day(self: Time) -> int`

### `fn hour(self: Time) -> int`

### `fn minute(self: Time) -> int`

### `fn second(self: Time) -> int`

### `fn nanosecond(self: Time) -> int`

### `fn millisecond(self: Time) -> int`

### `fn weekday(self: Time) -> Weekday`

### `fn year_day(self: Time) -> int`

1 to 366.

### `fn iso_week(self: Time) -> IsoWeek`

### `fn add(self: Time, d: int) -> Time`

`self` plus `d` nanoseconds (negative goes back).

### `fn sub(self: Time, o: Time) -> int`

Nanoseconds from `o` to `self`; saturates past ~292 years.

### `fn add_days(self: Time, n: int) -> Time`

Calendar days later, at the same time of day.

### `fn add_months(self: Time, n: int) -> Time`

Calendar months later, at the same time of day. A day past the end of the target month is clamped to its last day: Jan 31 + 1 month is Feb 28 (29 in a leap year), not Mar 3.

### `fn add_years(self: Time, n: int) -> Time`

Calendar years later; Feb 29 + 1 year is Feb 28.

### `fn before(self: Time, o: Time) -> bool`

### `fn after(self: Time, o: Time) -> bool`

### `fn equal(self: Time, o: Time) -> bool`

### `fn compare(self: Time, o: Time) -> int`

-1, 0 or 1.

### `fn truncate(self: Time, d: int) -> Time`

Rounded down to a multiple of `d` since the epoch (d <= 0 leaves it as is): truncate(MINUTE) drops seconds.

### `fn round(self: Time, d: int) -> Time`

Rounded to the nearest multiple of `d`, halves away from zero.

### `fn start_of_minute(self: Time) -> Time`

### `fn start_of_hour(self: Time) -> Time`

### `fn start_of_day(self: Time) -> Time`

### `fn start_of_week(self: Time) -> Time`

Monday 00:00 of this ISO week.

### `fn start_of_month(self: Time) -> Time`

### `fn start_of_year(self: Time) -> Time`

### `fn end_of_day(self: Time) -> Time`

The last nanosecond of the day, month and year: for inclusive range queries ("created <= end of day").

### `fn end_of_month(self: Time) -> Time`

### `fn end_of_year(self: Time) -> Time`

### `fn weekday(self: Date) -> Weekday`

### `fn year_day(self: Date) -> int`

### `fn iso_week(self: Date) -> IsoWeek`

### `fn is_leap_year(self: Date) -> bool`

### `fn add_days(self: Date, n: int) -> Date`

### `fn add_months(self: Date, n: int) -> Date`

Jan 31 + 1 month is Feb 28 (29 in a leap year).

### `fn add_years(self: Date, n: int) -> Date`

### `fn days_until(self: Date, o: Date) -> int`

Days from `self` to `o`: 1 for tomorrow, negative for the past.

### `fn years_until(self: Date, o: Date) -> int`

Whole years from `self` to `o`, counting a year only once its anniversary has passed: an age, a tenure.

### `fn start(self: Date) -> Time`

00:00:00 UTC on this date.

### `fn at(self: Date, hour: int, minute: int, second: int) -> result[Time, str]`

The instant at this date and a UTC time of day.

### `fn before(self: Date, o: Date) -> bool`

### `fn after(self: Date, o: Date) -> bool`

### `fn equal(self: Date, o: Date) -> bool`

### `fn compare(self: Date, o: Date) -> int`

### `fn start_of_month(self: Date) -> Date`

### `fn end_of_month(self: Date) -> Date`

### `fn iso(self: Date) -> str`

"2026-10-13" (ISO 8601).

### `fn parse_duration(s: str) -> result[int, str]`

A duration written as Go writes them -- "1h30m", "1.5s", "300ms", "-2m", "2us" -- plus "d" for 24-hour days ("7d"), the unit config files reach for. "0" alone is zero. err names what was wrong; values past ~292 years are refused, not wrapped.

### `fn format_duration(d: int) -> str`

A duration the way Go prints one and parse_duration reads it back: "1h30m0s", "1.5s", "300ms", "2µs", "0s".

### `gc struct Zone`

### `fn utc_zone() -> Zone`

UTC, as a Zone.

### `fn fixed_zone(name: str, offset_seconds: int) -> Zone`

A zone at a fixed offset (seconds east of UTC) that never changes.

### `fn load_zone(name: str) -> result[Zone, str]`

"UTC" and fixed zones need no database; anything else is read from it.

### `fn parse_tzif(name: str, b: bytes) -> result[Zone, str]`

RFC 8536: version 2 or later, whose 64-bit block and footer this reads (the 32-bit block before them is skipped).

### `fn parse_posix_tz(s: str) -> result[TzRule, str]`

### `fn offset_at(self: Zone, t: Time) -> int`

Seconds east of UTC at instant `t`.

### `fn is_dst_at(self: Zone, t: Time) -> bool`

### `fn abbrev_at(self: Zone, t: Time) -> str`

"CEST", "PST", "+0530": the abbreviation in use at `t`.

### `struct ZonedTime`

An instant together with the zone it is read in: what a person in that zone sees on a clock.

### `fn in_zone(self: Time, z: Zone) -> ZonedTime`

### `fn zoned(z: Zone, year: int, month: int, day: int, hour: int, minute: int, second: int, how: Disambiguation) -> result[Time, str]`

The instant for a wall time in `z`, by `how` when daylight saving makes it skipped or repeated.

### `fn date(self: ZonedTime) -> Date`

### `fn year(self: ZonedTime) -> int`

### `fn month(self: ZonedTime) -> int`

### `fn day(self: ZonedTime) -> int`

### `fn hour(self: ZonedTime) -> int`

### `fn minute(self: ZonedTime) -> int`

### `fn second(self: ZonedTime) -> int`

### `fn weekday(self: ZonedTime) -> Weekday`

### `fn abbrev(self: ZonedTime) -> str`

### `fn is_dst(self: ZonedTime) -> bool`

### `fn rfc3339(self: ZonedTime) -> str`

"2026-10-13T11:30:15+02:00".

### `fn format(self: ZonedTime, layout: str) -> str`

As Time.format, with %z the real offset (+0200) and %Z the zone's abbreviation (CEST).

### `fn add_days(self: ZonedTime, n: int) -> ZonedTime`

Calendar days later at the same wall time, across daylight-saving changes (a day is then 23 or 25 hours). A wall time that does not exist on the target day moves forward, as COMPATIBLE does.

### `fn add_months(self: ZonedTime, n: int) -> ZonedTime`

### `fn start_of_day(self: ZonedTime) -> ZonedTime`

Local midnight: the first instant of this date in the zone (01:00 where midnight is skipped).
